summary: Customer (Northport Bank) evaluated Redwood's capabilities for strict EU data residency and region pinning. Discussed hosting modes, private VPC vs hosted with region pinning, cross-border processing exceptions, KMS key control, sub-processors, SOC2/ISO evidence, and next steps for architecture diagrams and a benchmark run.
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-31
Time: 14:00 UTC
Duration: 42 minutes (recorded)
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE); Rajiv Singh (Redwood SE); Alice Morgan (Northport Head of Security); Tom Ellis (Platform Eng); Sarah Wu (Legal)

00:00 Maya Chen: hey everyone, thanks for joining, i'll hand it over quick intro then rajiv will jump into the region pinning flow, uh apologies if there's any background noise
00:12 Alice Morgan: hey maya, thanks, we've got about 40 minutes, looking to validate residency guarantees and the legal implications for our EU customers
00:25 Rajiv Singh: cool, i'll start with a high-level: Redwood supports three modes — hosted api, dedicated pools, and private (vpc/on-prem). For data residency we offer region pinning which routes requests to region-specific capacity and we also have private control plane options so sensitive processing can be kept inside customer VPCs
00:38 Tom Ellis: couple quick Qs up front — is region pinning at request level or at model level? we need EU-only for PCI-related prompts
00:52 Rajiv Singh: good question. we can do per-route pinning; so you can pin specific endpoints to eu-west-1 for example. it's implemented in the smart routing layer. note there are also fallbacks for capacity — we can configure policy to fail closed (reject) rather than fail open to US, that's configurable in the routing policy
01:15 Alice Morgan: important for us is that no token content or logs leave the EU, plus audit logs and k-v cache evicted in-region. how do you guarantee that?
01:30 Rajiv Singh: we keep separate regional clusters and storage partitions. for hosted mode we provide EU-only tenancy where all compute and storage stays in-region and we do not replicate logs across regions by default. there are some internal control plane messages for orchestration but we can provide the private control plane option so control plane traffic is on your VPC — less cross-border telemetry
01:55 Sarah Wu: legal note — what about lawful requests/sub-processors? we need the sub-processor list and we need contract language in the DPA that restricts cross-border processing except with prior consent
02:10 Maya Chen: absolutely — we'll share the current sub-processor list and an executed DPA template. we also have a CSV of subprocessors per region, i'll add that to the security pack
02:25 Tom Ellis: can you speak to KMS and key ownership? we need customer-managed keys and we can't have Redwood hold plaintext keys for EU-only workloads
02:38 Rajiv Singh: yes, we support bring-your-own-key (BYOK) via KMS integrations. For cloud-hosted customers you can provision an EU KMS in your account and we only hold references. For private deployments you keep the keys on-prem/HSM, we never see plaintext. a note: for hosted dedicated pools we can enable CMEK with your KMS — keys are regional
03:00 Alice Morgan: does that extend to model artifacts and embeddings persisted for caching? any chance those escape region boundaries for indexing or analytics?
03:14 Rajiv Singh: model weights are in the serving pool; embeddings and cache entries are stored in-region for pinned routes. analytics aggregates can be redacted or limited; we'll show the settings in the diagram we'll send. small caveat — if you request third-party evaluation that includes cross-region compute we need consent — but standard inference and logs are kept in-region when pinned
03:40 Maya Chen: i've seen a few customers ask about SOC 2 and ISO. we are SOC 2 Type II and ISO27001 certified — i'll attach the certs. any specific evidence you need?
03:53 Alice Morgan: A TOC and the control mappings would be useful; also pen test results summary. we'll want to validate how RBAC and SSO tie into your console and API tokens
04:05 Rajiv Singh: RBAC integrates with SAML/SSO; we support SCIM provisioning and fine-grained roles for route-level and model-level permissioning. API keys can also be scoped. for audit logs we retain token-level traces and admin actions and those can be exported to your logging bucket in the EU
04:30 Tom Ellis: about cross-border processing — what about background jobs like batch fine-tuning or feature extraction that run in US by default? we need assurance those can be pinned
04:45 Rajiv Singh: batch jobs can be scheduled on region-specific clusters. some orchestration tasks default to control-plane in US but with Private mode we can move the control plane to your EU region or on-prem. we will call that out in the architecture doc
05:10 Sarah Wu: legal: if Redwood receives a lawful request in US that affects EU data, what's your approach? do you notify us? how's conflict of laws handled?
05:25 Maya Chen: we have a notification policy for customer data requests and will contest requests where permissible; the DPA covers notification and legal assistance. we'll loop in our legal team on any cross-border notice obligations
05:40 Alice Morgan: can you share your sub-processor list now or is that in the pack?
05:45 Maya Chen: in the pack; i'll attach. quick note — we use some cloud infra providers (bigcloud) and analytics vendors; those are on the list and regionally scoped
06:00 Tom Ellis: latency vs cost trade-offs — if we pin everything to EU, do we pay more or see lower capacity on some models?
06:12 Rajiv Singh: depends on model and capacity in-region. heavyweight models may be scarcer in some regions so either we run smaller quantized variants or we provision dedicated capacity. Redwood Optimize can recommend quantization and batching profiles to meet latency/cost targets. dedicated pools also give predictable throughput albeit additional commit costs
06:40 Alice Morgan: curious about fallback policies — you said fail closed possible. can you walk through examples?
06:48 Rajiv Singh: fail closed returns an error if EU capacity not available; fail open routes to nearest compatible region (which you can disallow for certain routes). we also support canary policies: try EU first and if latency exceeds threshold then route to dedicated EU-only pool or return an explicit 429-style signal for client-side retry
07:20 Tom Ellis: how are audit logs handled for admin actions — do you provide immutable logs? can they be exported to our SIEM in EU?
07:32 Rajiv Singh: yes, audit logs are immutable append-only in-region and we support push to customer-owned S3/GS buckets in the EU. we can also stream to your SIEM via syslog or HTTP endpoint behind VPC peering
07:50 Sarah Wu: any subcontractors outside EU we should worry about? e.g., support teams that might view metadata?
07:58 Maya Chen: support access is RBAC-controlled and goes through a ticket workflow; we can block access to production logs for certain tiers and require customer-approved breakout for any data access. support staff locations are listed in the sub-processor list
08:20 Alice Morgan: what's your retention policy for transcripts/utterances? we'll be sending user queries including PII sometimes
08:30 Rajiv Singh: default retention is 90 days for request/response payloads and 365 days for aggregated metrics, but retention is configurable per customer and per-route. we can set EU-only retention and automatic purge policies. if you need shorter retention for PCI scopes we can enforce that via config
09:00 Tom Ellis: are there any parts of the control plane that still make US calls even if pinned? you mentioned orchestration earlier
09:12 Rajiv Singh: minimal control-plane metadata may hit our central control plane for coordination, but sensitive payloads are never sent. for customers with strict compliance we recommend Private mode where the control plane is inside your VPC and orchestration occurs in-region
09:35 Alice Morgan: ok let's talk about sub-processors and the DPA language for cross-border pre-approval. we want explicit clause that disallows cross-border unless written consent and documented exception
09:50 Maya Chen: understood; we'll propose DPA wording and show the subprocessors and region scopes. we already support contractual restrictions in enterprise agreements
10:05 Sarah Wu: encryption in transit and at rest — do you use TLS 1.2/1.3? and which ciphers?
10:12 Rajiv Singh: we use TLS 1.3 by default, strong cipher suites; at rest we use AES-256 and CMEK for customer keys. I'll have the security pack include cipher lists and key rotation windows
10:35 Tom Ellis: are any analytics or telemetry sent to third-party analytics providers that are US-hosted?
10:40 Maya Chen: telemetry can be restricted. by default some anonymized telemetry helps us optimize routing but for enterprise EU-only customers we can disable third-party analytics and keep telemetry in-region
11:00 Alice Morgan: for the benchmark we want to run a subset of our prompt types in EU pinning and measure P95 latency and token cost. what's the instrumentation?
11:12 Rajiv Singh: we'll provide a benchmark script that hits pinned endpoints and returns per-request latency, token counts, and cost estimates. we can run it in a dedicated EU pool to replicate production constraints
11:35 Tom Ellis: can you also include KV cache visibility? we don't want long-lived caches holding PII across sessions
11:40 Rajiv Singh: yes, KV cache is configurable — TTLs and eviction policies can be set per-route; we can disable prefix caching for sensitive routes or encrypt cache blobs with customer keys
12:05 Maya Chen: quick note on sub-processors — redwood uses a handful of infra partners and cloud providers, most are regionally bound, but we'll send the detailed list and their data centers
12:20 Sarah Wu: regarding lawful requests again, we may want a flow that requires Redwood to notify us and allow us to challenge where possible; is that in your standard DPA?
12:30 Maya Chen: yes, notification and coordination are standard but we'll flag the clause and propose stronger notice windows if needed
12:45 Alice Morgan: any differences between hosted dedicated and private for our use-case? we're leaning to a hosted but with strict EU-only guarantees — is that feasible without Private?
12:58 Rajiv Singh: hosted EU tenancy can meet many requirements but Private gives the highest assurance because control plane and orchestration stay in your network. hosted dedicated with strict routing and fail-closed policies may be sufficient if you accept vendor-managed control plane bounded to EU — we'll diagram the trade-offs
13:25 Tom Ellis: curious about subprocessor change notifications — do you notify customers before adding a new subprocessor that will see customer data?
13:35 Maya Chen: yes we have a 30-day notice for major subprocessor changes that affect data handling; minor infra swaps that don't touch data plane are in our standard change log but we can expand notification on request
13:50 Sarah Wu: for SSO, we require SAML with enforced MFA and SCIM provisioning. does Redwood support that?
13:58 Rajiv Singh: yep, SAML SSO + SCIM supported, MFA enforced via your IdP. roles map to Redwood RBAC and can be scoped to per-route permissions
14:20 Alice Morgan: ok let's recap next steps and owners before we wrap
14:25 Maya Chen: recap: i'll send the SOC2+ISO pack, sub-processor list, and DPA language (Maya). Rajiv will send architecture diagram and sample config for region pinning + benchmark script (Rajiv). Northport to send list of EU-only workloads (Tom). follow-up KMS/SSO dive on 2026-04-07 tentatively
14:45 Tom Ellis: sounds good thanks everyone
14:50 Alice Morgan: thanks, talk soon
14:55 Maya Chen: thanks all, we'll follow up in email with attachments. bye
notes: Customer strongly prefers EU-only processing for regulated customer subsets (PCI / PII)
Redwood offered multiple options: hosted EU tenancy, hosted dedicated with fail-closed, private control plane; recommended follow-up benchmark and architecture doc
Legal wants explicit DPA language for cross-border processing and sub-processor pre-approval
